findings.summary: Page 2 renders as a broken near-empty page containing only an orphaned three-line code block with the rest of the sheet blank.
findings.evidence: Entire page 2 body is the single block "IFS=: read -r a b c <<< \"$line\" / # prefix applies to this read only / # no save/restore cleanup needed", occupying roughly the top 7% of the page; the remaining ~1100px of ruled paper below it is empty.
findings.fix: Merge this overflow block back into page 1's "The Shell Reads a Line" layout (or pull following content forward) so no page ships with a single orphaned block; if the content genuinely does not fit, rebalance the part's page breaks before render.

findings.summary: ANSI-C quoting `$'...'` is used in two page-1 examples but is not defined until page 3.
findings.evidence: Page 1 code: "$'\\t'                  # a real tab" and "$'\\x41' $'\\u00e9'      # A and e-acute". The definition "`$'...'` is ANSI-C quoting: `\n` `\t` `\x41` `\u00e9` interpreted." appears on page 3 under "2. Dollar-Quoting".
findings.fix: Move the `"$HOME"/bin/'my app'` + `$'\t'` + `$'\x41'` code block from page 1 to page 3, placing it under the "2. Dollar-Quoting" bullets.

findings.summary: The entire page is a single `IFS=: read -r` idiom whose three prerequisites — IFS, `read -r`, and the here-string — are not introduced until page 4.
findings.evidence: Page 2 ("The Shell Reads a Line (cont.)") contains exactly one block: ["IFS=: read -r a b c <<< \"$line\"", "# prefix applies to this read only", "# no save/restore cleanup needed"]. "`IFS` = Internal Field Separator." and "`-r` is mandatory: keeps backslashes intact." first appear on page 4.
findings.fix: Move this code block to page 4 directly under "3. Reading Lines", after the `IFS` basics bullets and the `while IFS= read -r line` loop, and either fill page 2 with the chapter-1 order-of-operations material it is titled for or drop the page.

findings.summary: A three-bullet block about fork-free path surgery sits on page 6 with no antecedent — the `${path##*/}` construct it describes does not appear until page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 6 bullets: "Safe with newlines in filenames.", "No fork means no process-creation cost.", "A loop of `basename` pays milliseconds per iteration." Nothing on page 6 mentions `basename`, `${path##*/}`, or trimming; "2. Path Surgery" with "${path##*/}    # basename, no fork" is on page 7.
findings.fix: Move these three bullets to page 7 immediately after the "2. Path Surgery" code block, or merge them into the page-8 "Zero Forks" callout that already makes the same point.

findings.summary: The colon-vs-no-colon rule is stated before any of the default-value operators it modifies have been shown.
findings.evidence: Page 6, second block: "No colon = only UNSET triggers the default.", "An empty variable stays empty.", "Same switch applies across all these operators." — placed before the chapter-opening heading "1. Braces Disambiguate" and before the "2. Default Operators" table row ["`${v:-d}`","d if unset or empty"]. "these operators" has no referent at that point.
findings.fix: Delete this bullet block from the top of page 6 and fold its three lines into the "3. The Colon Switch" section, immediately above the unset/empty/`x` comparison table.

findings.summary: An indirect-expansion example is shown a full page before indirect expansion is defined.
findings.evidence: Page 6 code: ["for n in \"${!APP_@}\"; do", "  printf '%s=%s\\n' \"$n\" \"${!n}\"", "done          # enumerate config vars"]. The defining bullets "`${!var}` is indirect: var='HOME' yields `$HOME`." and "`${!prefix*}` and `${!prefix@}` list names by prefix." are on page 7 under "4. Length & Indirection".
findings.fix: Move this code block to page 7, directly beneath the "4. Length & Indirection" bullets that define `${!var}` and `${!prefix@}`.

findings.summary: Case-modification and `@`-transform operators are commented on before the table that introduces them, and section 5 is printed ahead of section 4.
findings.evidence: Page 7 ends with bullets "Case modification needs Bash 4+.", "`${v@Q}` is the correct way to build a string for `eval` or `ssh`.", "`${v@A}` emits a reusable declaration.", then heading "5. Element-Wise On Arrays". The table defining them — ["`${v^}` `${v^^}`","upper first / all"] … ["`${v@Q}`","shell-safe quoted"] — is headed "4. Case And @ Transforms" on page 8.
findings.fix: Pull the "4. Case And @ Transforms" heading and table back onto page 7 ahead of its three explanatory bullets, so the chapter runs 1→2→3→4→5 and no `@` operator is discussed before it is shown.

findings.summary: Section numbers restart at each page boundary rather than at each chapter, so most pages carry two sections with the same number.
findings.evidence: Page 4 has "4. What Actually Splits" and "4. Splitting On Purpose"; page 7 has "5. Positionals & Specials" and "5. Element-Wise On Arrays"; page 8 has "1. Declare And Index" and "1. Loading From Files"; page 9 has "4. Forwarding" and "4. Associative Arrays"; page 10 has "6. Legitimate `\"$*\"`" and "6. Exit Status".
findings.fix: Number sections continuously per chapter (carry the count across the page break instead of resetting at the top of each page), so no page shows the same number twice.

findings.summary: The handbook states that an unquoted redirection target produces an "ambiguous redirect" error unconditionally, when bash only errors if the word expands to zero or more than one word.
findings.evidence: "> $file    # unquoted: ambiguous redirect" (page 1) and "Unquoted redirection: 'ambiguous redirect' error." (page 10). With `file=/tmp/out`, `> $file` works fine; bash reports "ambiguous redirect" only when the expansion is empty or splits into multiple words.
findings.fix: Reword both places to state the condition, e.g. `> $file  # ambiguous redirect if $file is empty or has spaces` and "Unquoted redirect word: empty or multi-word -> 'ambiguous redirect'."

findings.summary: The `'it'\''s'` escape trick is demonstrated before the rule that makes it necessary.
findings.evidence: Page 1 shows "echo 'it'\\''s'   # -> it's" two blocks before the heading "6. Single Quotes" and its bullet "A single quote cannot appear inside, by any means."
findings.fix: Reorder page 1 so the "6. Single Quotes" heading and its three bullets come first, then the `'it'\''s'` code block as the worked answer to the restriction just stated.

findings.summary: `!` is listed as a live character inside double quotes without noting it only applies when history expansion is enabled, which is off in scripts.
findings.evidence: "Live characters: `$`, backtick, `\`, and `!`." Bash performs history expansion on `!` inside double quotes only when history expansion is enabled — default on in interactive shells, off in non-interactive scripts, where `echo "Hello!"` is fully literal.
findings.fix: Change the bullet to "Live characters: `$`, backtick, `\` — plus `!` in interactive shells only (history expansion; off in scripts)."

findings.summary: Chapter-1 debugging tooling is dropped into the middle of the quoting chapter, between two quoting sections.
findings.evidence: Page 3 order: heading "7. Backslash & Joining" → its bullets → code ["set -x                    # trace after expansion", "printf '[%s]\\n' $var      # count the arguments"] → heading "1. Double Quotes". The surrounding sections are about quoting; this block belongs to the expansion-pipeline chapter.
findings.fix: Move the `set -x` / `printf '[%s]\n' $var` block to page 1 beside the "Memorise One Sentence" callout, which is where the pipeline it debugs is taught.

findings.summary: The deferral sidebox points the reader to the wrong chapter for `"$@"`.
findings.evidence: Page 3 sidebox "Deferred": "Full treatment in the arrays chapter." The arrays page (page 8) only shows "\"${@:2}\"          # all args after the first"; the actual treatment is the next chapter, page 9, "\"$@\" vs $*: Passing Arguments".
findings.fix: Change the sidebox line to "Full treatment in the \"$@\" vs $* chapter."

findings.summary: The read loop is labelled "the only correct loop" although it silently drops a final line that lacks a trailing newline.
findings.evidence: "while IFS= read -r line; do / printf '%s\n' "$line" / done < file        # the only correct loop". `read` returns non-zero at EOF after storing a partial last line, so the body never runs for an unterminated final line.
findings.fix: Either change the comment to "the correct quoting for this loop" or use the complete idiom: `while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do ... done < file`.

findings.summary: The third cell of the small three-cell comparison table under the "for x in $(cat file)" section overruns its cell, unlike the two bordered cells beside it.
findings.evidence: Cells "$x: zero args" and "\"$x\": one empty arg" are fully boxed and centered, while the third cell's text "x='' then f $x vs f \"$x\"" starts flush against the divider, wraps with \"$x\" onto a second line, and runs to the table edge with no closing right border drawn.
findings.fix: Shorten the third cell's label (e.g. "x='': f $x vs f \"$x\"") or widen that column so the text fits inside a properly closed cell like its siblings.

findings.summary: The default-operators table describes `${v:+alt}` as "alt only if set", omitting the non-empty requirement the colon imposes, contradicting the page's own colon rule.
findings.evidence: Table row "`${v:+alt}` | alt only if set", while the same page states "No colon = only UNSET triggers the default." With `v=` (set but empty), `${v:+alt}` expands to nothing; it is `${v+alt}` that means "only if set".
findings.fix: Change the row to "alt if set and non-empty" (and optionally add `${v+alt}` = "alt if set, even if empty").

findings.summary: The "prefer `[[ ... ]]`" recommendation is given a page before the `[ $x = y ]` failure that motivates it.
findings.evidence: Page 9 closes with "Prefer `[[ ... ]]` in Bash.", "No word splitting or globbing on operands.", "Quote RIGHT side of `==` unless globbing." Page 10 then presents the problem: "[ $x = y ]      # ERROR if x is empty" under "2. Test Syntax".
findings.fix: Move the three `[[ ... ]]` bullets from the end of page 9 to page 10 immediately after the "2. Test Syntax" code block, so the failure precedes the fix.

findings.summary: The closing callout claims quotes are optional in array subscripts, but an unquoted subscript in an ordinary command word is glob-expanded, which can silently unset the wrong variable.
findings.evidence: "Inside `$(( ))` and array subscripts, splitting does not happen. Quotes are optional there." The handbook itself writes `unset arr[1]` (page 8); with a file named `arr1` in the cwd, `unset arr[1]` pathname-expands to `unset arr1`, and with `nullglob` the word vanishes entirely — this is ShellCheck SC2184, "Quote arguments to unset so they're not glob expanded."
findings.fix: Qualify the callout: splitting/globbing are suppressed inside `${arr[i]}` and `$(( ))`, but subscripts appearing as command arguments must be quoted — `unset 'arr[1]'`, `test -v 'arr[1]'` — and update the page 8 bullet to `unset 'arr[1]'`.

findings.summary: Two counterintuitive exit-status claims are asserted with no code showing the failure or the fix.
findings.evidence: Page 10 bullets: "`export VAR=$(cmd)` masks cmd's exit status.", "Split assignment from export when checking failures.", "`set -e` does not fire in command substitutions." — the surrounding sections all carry code blocks; these do not.
findings.fix: Add a three-line code block beside them, e.g. `export VAR=$(false); echo $?   # 0` / `VAR=$(false) || exit 1` / `export VAR`.
